summary:
Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data is an AI-powered agricultural decision-support system designed to help farmers adapt crop rotation strategies to changing environmental conditions.

The platform combines NASA POWER climate data, including temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, humidity, and wind speed, with farm-specific information and agricultural research. Using an AI-driven workflow, it analyzes these inputs and generates three tailored crop rotation strategies, explaining their potential benefits, risks, and supporting evidence.

Field Shift addresses the challenge by transforming Earth observation data into practical, farm-level agricultural insights. Its modular architecture also allows future integration of additional NASA datasets, such as SMAP soil moisture and MODIS vegetation indices, to enrich environmental analysis.

The project is important because climate variability and water scarcity threaten agricultural productivity, particularly in vulnerable farming regions. By connecting satellite observations with AI-assisted decision-making, Field Shift aims to support more informed crop planning, improve resource management, and strengthen agricultural resilience.
details:
Project Overview and How It Works

Field Shift is an AI-powered agricultural decision-support platform that helps farmers explore crop rotation strategies based on environmental conditions and farm-specific information.

The farmer enters a farm profile through a Flutter application, including its location, soil characteristics, current and previous crops, irrigation practices, available water, and farming priorities.

The backend uses NASA POWER API to retrieve climate data for the farm's geographical location, including temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, relative humidity, and wind speed. Python and Pandas process and analyze this data to produce meaningful climate indicators.

An AI-driven workflow, orchestrated using LangGraph, then combines the environmental analysis, farm profile, and agricultural research retrieved through Tavily Search. A Groq-hosted Large Language Model generates three alternative crop rotation strategies. Each strategy includes a proposed crop sequence, rationale, potential benefits, risks, and supporting evidence. A validation stage checks the basic structure and consistency of the generated output.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Field Shift aims to make satellite-based environmental information more actionable for farmers. Instead of presenting raw climate data, it translates environmental indicators into understandable agricultural recommendations.

Its intended benefits include:

  • Supporting crop planning under changing climate conditions.
  • Helping farmers consider water availability and resource efficiency.
  • Encouraging crop diversification and more informed crop rotation decisions.
  • Providing multiple strategies so farmers can compare alternatives based on their priorities.
  • Making Earth observation data more accessible for agricultural decision-making.

The long-term impact is to support more climate-resilient farming, improve resource management, and help reduce the risks associated with unsuitable crop choices.

Tools and Technologies

Frontend: Flutter and Dart.

Backend: Python and FastAPI.

NASA Data: NASA POWER API for climate observations and derived environmental indicators.

Data Processing: Pandas and NumPy.

AI and Orchestration: Groq LLM, LangChain, and LangGraph.

Agricultural Research: Tavily Search.

Data Validation: Pydantic and custom Python validation logic.

The solution is software-based and does not require specialized hardware. It is designed to work with satellite and farm-provided data.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Field Shift is the integration of Earth observation data, farm-specific information, agricultural research, and generative AI into a single decision-support workflow.

Rather than relying on predefined crop rotation templates, the system generates alternative strategies dynamically from the available inputs. Its modular architecture separates data collection, analysis, research, generation, and validation, making it easier to introduce additional environmental datasets and analytical capabilities.

Factors Considered

The project considers several factors that influence agricultural decisions:

  • Geographic location and local climate conditions.
  • Temperature, rainfall, solar radiation, humidity, and wind patterns.
  • Soil type and farmer-provided soil measurements.
  • Current crop and previous crop history.
  • Irrigation method and available water.
  • Farmer priorities, such as water efficiency, soil health, productivity, and climate resilience.
  • Agricultural research and supporting evidence.
  • Data availability, spatial resolution, and the limitations of satellite-derived estimates.

These factors help the system generate more context-aware recommendations while recognizing that AI-generated strategies require further agronomic validation and local field testing before implementation.
